::: {.exercise-lead}
I use the 2022 road accident records to look at where accidents were reported in Greater Bangkok, which reports involved deaths, and how the pattern changed through the year.
:::

[View the short presentation](take-home-exercise-01-summary.qmd)

## 1. What I want to find out

I chose Greater Bangkok so I could look at the city and its surrounding provinces together. The 2022 data cover a full year, which makes it possible to compare the months.

There are six questions I want to explore:

- Where were most accidents recorded?
- Which roads make up the main concentration?
- Which months had more accidents?
- Do the places with the most reports also have the most fatal reports, and how do time of day and vehicle type matter?
- Did nearby accidents happen close together in time more often than expected?
- Could missing locations change what the maps and charts show?

I check the records before making the maps. Then I look for places with many reports and test whether nearby accidents happened close together in time. To judge how dangerous a road is, I would also need to know how much traffic it carries.

## 2. The data

| Data | What I use it for |
|---|---|
| [Thailand Road Accident 2019–2022 on Kaggle](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/thaweewatboy/thailand-road-accident-2019-2022) | Locations, dates, vehicle categories, weather and recorded casualties. I use only 2022. Each row is an accident report, which may involve several vehicles or people. |
| [geoBoundaries country downloads](https://www.geoboundaries.org/countryDownloads.html) | Select **Thailand → ADM1** for provincial boundaries. I use the boundaries representing 2017 to define the study area and assign reports to provinces. |
| [OpenStreetMap: eastern Bangkok](https://www.openstreetmap.org/#map=12/13.7330/100.7140) | Browse the roads around Routes 7 and 9. The analysis uses roads as mapped on **1 January 2022**; the linked map shows today's roads. |

The accident data and boundaries were downloaded on 11 September 2026, and the roads on 17 September. The accident data come from a compilation of Ministry of Transport records covering **highways, rural roads and expressways**. They do not cover every accident on every local street. [Source: Ministry of Transport](https://datagov.mot.go.th/dataset/roadaccident).

Here, Greater Bangkok means **Bangkok, Nonthaburi, Pathum Thani, Nakhon Pathom, Samut Prakan and Samut Sakhon**, following the National Statistical Office's [Bangkok and Vicinities grouping](https://www.nso.go.th/public/e-book/Statistical-Yearbook/SYB-2025/110/).

The study runs from 1 January to 31 December 2022, using the date of the accident. A report submitted later still belongs to the day the accident happened. I treat the times as local Thai time, although the source does not state the time zone.

I combine the six provinces into one study area, so the analysis can cross their internal borders. WGS 84 / UTM zone 47N (EPSG:32647) lets me measure distances in metres. I start with straight-line distances, then follow the roads for a closer look at eastern Bangkok.











## 3. Checking the records

First, I kept the 2022 records. I then checked their dates and locations, removed records that could not be placed on a map, and kept those inside the six provinces.


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}


|Records                          | Number|
|:--------------------------------|------:|
|All years in the downloaded file | 81,735|
|From 2022                        | 21,032|
|From 2022, with usable locations | 20,843|
|Inside Greater Bangkok           |  3,599|


:::
:::


This leaves **3,599 accident records** for the map. All the dates could be read, and there were no completely duplicated records. No coordinates were outside the valid latitude/longitude ranges or recorded as (0, 0). I also checked the boundary shapes for invalid or empty geometry before using them to select the points.

None of the mapped reports has a missing or negative injury or death count. I call a report fatal when it records at least one death. The mapped records include **159 fatal reports and 177 deaths**. A zero means no death was recorded in this file; the source does not tell me whether casualties were followed up later.

### 3.1 Missing locations

There are **189 records without coordinates**. All are listed as accidents in Bangkok. I checked which agency reported them to see whether the missing locations were spread across the data.


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](take-home-exercise-01_files/figure-html/th01-missingness-1.png){width=864}
:::
:::


All 189 came from the Expressway Authority. They make up **43.1% of its 439 Bangkok reports**, compared with no missing locations in the other two agencies' Bangkok records. This means the map leaves out a substantial part of the Expressway Authority's reports. I keep these records for the monthly comparison because their dates are still available, but cannot place them on the map. Two of the excluded reports record a death, so the later severity maps and comparisons also leave those out.

### 3.2 Repeated or conflicting locations

There are 321 records at coordinates already used by another record. Several accidents can happen at the same place, so I keep them. Two pairs have both the same location and the same accident time, but different record numbers. I cannot tell whether these are duplicate reports. I keep them in the main analysis and later check whether removing them changes the result.

A few records have coordinates that disagree with their province names. I use their plotted locations to decide whether they belong in the study area. This excludes four records listed under the six provinces and includes ten listed elsewhere. The boundary data are older than the accident records, so I cannot assume every disagreement is a recording error.

## 4. Where were accidents recorded?

Each dot is an accident record. Records at the same location overlap, so one visible dot can represent several accidents.


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](take-home-01/figures/locations.png){fig-alt='Map of six Greater Bangkok provinces with 3,599 recorded accident locations in 2022, showing linear concentrations and uneven spatial coverage.' width=720}
:::
:::


The dots follow several long routes through Bangkok and towards the surrounding provinces. This fits the dataset's focus on highways, rural roads and expressways. Bangkok has the largest number of mapped records, followed by Samut Prakan. Areas with fewer dots should not automatically be seen as safer: some roads may be outside this reporting system, and we do not know how much traffic each road carries.


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}


|Province      | Accident records| Share (%)|
|:-------------|----------------:|---------:|
|Bangkok       |             1802|      50.1|
|Samut Prakan  |              671|      18.6|
|Pathum Thani  |              491|      13.6|
|Samut Sakhon  |              323|       9.0|
|Nonthaburi    |              174|       4.8|
|Nakhon Pathom |              138|       3.8|


:::
:::


Bangkok accounts for **1,802 records**, about half of those on the map. Samut Prakan follows with **671**. These counts use the recorded coordinates to assign each accident to a province.

## 5. When were more accidents recorded?

Longer months have more days for accidents to occur. To make the comparison fairer, I divide each month's total by its number of days.

The solid line uses the records shown on the map. The dashed line adds the 189 reports with missing locations. Their province names place them in Bangkok, although I cannot check their exact positions.




::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](take-home-01/figures/monthly.png){fig-alt='Monthly accident records per day. Both the mapped records and the comparison including reports with missing locations peak in October.' width=720}
:::
:::


**October has the highest count: 394 mapped records, or about 12.7 per day.** November has fewer records than December, but more per day because it is a shorter month. April also stands out compared with March and May.

Adding the reports with missing locations raises the figures slightly but leaves the same broad pattern: more accidents were recorded towards the end of the year. The location gaps therefore do not explain that increase on their own. The chart does not tell us whether changes in traffic, road conditions or reporting caused it.





### 5.1 Does the time of day change the picture?

I split the day into four equal six-hour periods to see when more accidents were reported and how often they involved a death.


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](take-home-01/figures/time-severity.png){fig-alt='Two bar charts: overnight has 644 reports, fewer than the other six-hour periods, but 8.5 percent involve a death, the largest share.' width=800}
:::
:::


Midnight to 6 am has the fewest reports, but **55 of its 644 reports involve a death (8.5%)**. During the daytime, the share is around 2 to 2.5%. For emergency planning, I would consider how often accidents involved a death as well as how many were reported.

To check whether different vehicle types might explain this, I compared motorcycle reports during the day and at night. At night, 58 of 213 were fatal (27.2%), compared with 22 of 193 during the day (11.4%). I use 6 pm to 6 am for nighttime; this is based on the clock, not measured darkness. The nighttime share is higher even within this group, although differences in traffic, speed or reporting could still matter.

### 5.2 Which vehicle groups stand out?

The source gives each report one vehicle category. It does not list every vehicle involved, so I compare reports carrying each label without assuming which vehicle or person caused the accident.


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](take-home-01/figures/vehicle-severity.png){fig-alt='Motorcycle reports have the highest fatal share among the six common named vehicle categories: 80 of 406, or 19.7 percent.' width=720}
:::
:::


Cars and pickups appear more often in the file. Motorcycles account for 406 reports (11.3% of the total), yet **80 of the 159 fatal reports (50.3%)** carry the motorcycle label.

The same difference appears within both agencies that record motorcycle accidents. In Department of Highways records, 17.6% of motorcycle reports are fatal, compared with 2.5% of other reports. For the Department of Rural Roads, the figures are 24.2% and 8.5%. These percentages describe accidents in the file; they cannot tell us the chance of dying on a motorcycle journey. Another 399 reports use the vehicle label "other", which limits the comparison.



## 6. Where do the main concentrations appear?

Overlapping dots make it hard to see where there are more reports. Kernel density estimation (KDE) smooths them into a map, with darker areas where reports are more concentrated. This is the first-order part of the analysis: looking at how the number of events varies from place to place.

I use a Gaussian kernel with a 2 km bandwidth. This spreads each accident's contribution around its location, fading with distance. The bandwidth controls how much the map is smoothed. I chose 2 km to look at broad areas and also try 1 km and 4 km to see how much the choice matters.

The map is divided into 250 m cells. Near the outer boundary, I correct for the part of the smoothing that would fall outside the study area. Accidents outside the boundary are still missing from the data. Smoothing also spreads colour over land between roads, so this map shows the broad density of reports per square kilometre. It cannot identify the risk on an individual road section. [Method: spatstat KDE documentation](https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/spatstat.explore/html/density.ppp.html).


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](take-home-01/figures/density.png){fig-alt='Smoothed density of recorded accidents across the six Greater Bangkok provinces, using a two kilometre bandwidth.' width=720}
:::
:::


Eastern Bangkok has the darkest patch, near 100.714°E, 13.733°N. The estimated density there is about 9.3 records per km² over the year. Other patches extend into the surrounding provinces. I would use these areas to decide where to look more closely, then check the original records to find the roads and junctions involved. Differences in traffic and reporting coverage may explain some of the shading. The missing expressway locations also leave gaps.

### 6.1 Does the smoothing choice change the picture?


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](take-home-exercise-01_files/figure-html/th01-bandwidth-check-1.png){fig-alt='Three density maps using one, two and four kilometre bandwidths with the same colour scale.' width=864}
:::
:::


Eastern Bangkok stands out in all three maps. With more smoothing, the peak drops from 21.7 to 9.3 to 4.0 records per km², and nearby patches merge. The broad location stays similar, but its outline and peak value depend on the bandwidth. I would be cautious about drawing a precise hotspot boundary from any one of these maps. Whether the pattern is statistically unusual needs a separate test.

### 6.2 Which roads make up the eastern Bangkok concentration?

The broad density map made me want to look more closely at eastern Bangkok. I take a 10 km by 10 km area around its strongest peak and match the reports to the roads. Of the 442 reports here, 426 have usable matches. I leave out 16 where nearby roads at different levels make the choice unclear.



Route 7 accounts for 245 of the matched reports and Route 9 for 122. Together, that is about 86%. Network KDE smooths these reports along connected roads. Using a 1 km smoothing distance, the map shows which stretches contribute to the broader patch we saw earlier.


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](take-home-01/figures/roads.png){fig-alt='Road density in a ten kilometre square in eastern Bangkok, showing concentrations along Routes 7 and 9.' width=720}
:::
:::


The darkest stretch lies on Route 7, east of its junction with Route 9. I would start a closer review there and on the connecting ramps. All the reports in this small area come from the Department of Highways, so the quieter local streets are not a fair comparison. The map also cannot tell us the chance of an accident per journey without traffic counts.

### 6.3 Do fatal reports concentrate in the same places?

I compare the locations of all reports with the 159 that involved a death. Both maps use the same 2 km smoothing. Dividing the density values by each group's number of reports lets me compare where they concentrate on a shared colour scale.


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](take-home-01/figures/severity-geography.png){fig-alt='Comparable density maps: all reports peak in eastern Bangkok, while reports involving a death have their strongest two-kilometre smoothed peak in Pathum Thani.' width=900}
:::
:::


The strongest peak is in **Pathum Thani** for fatal reports, compared with eastern Bangkok for all reports. Nonthaburi and Samut Prakan also stand out more. The colours show where reports within each group concentrate, not a road user's chance of dying. With only 159 fatal reports, a few locations and the amount of smoothing can have more influence on the map's shape.

The province totals make the difference easier to see:


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}


|Province      | Reports| Fatal reports| Share of all reports (%)| Share of fatal reports (%)|
|:-------------|-------:|-------------:|------------------------:|--------------------------:|
|Pathum Thani  |     491|            41|                     13.6|                       25.8|
|Samut Prakan  |     671|            40|                     18.6|                       25.2|
|Bangkok       |   1,802|            27|                     50.1|                       17.0|
|Nonthaburi    |     174|            26|                      4.8|                       16.4|
|Samut Sakhon  |     323|            19|                      9.0|                       11.9|
|Nakhon Pathom |     138|             6|                      3.8|                        3.8|


:::
:::


Bangkok accounts for **50.1% of all reports but 17.0% of fatal reports**. Pathum Thani and Samut Prakan together account for just over half of fatal reports, although they have about a third of all reports. Nonthaburi has relatively few reports overall, but 26 of its 174 reports are fatal. Looking only at totals would give it less attention.

I checked the Department of Highways records separately to see whether agency coverage explained the difference. The fatal share is still 1.3% in Bangkok and 12.6% in Nonthaburi. I would investigate those locations, but would need to account for differences in roads, vehicles and reporting before comparing how safe the provinces are.

## 7. Did the concentrations move during the year?

The monthly chart showed more reports late in the year. Did those extra reports come from the same places? I split the year into four quarters to make the maps easier to compare than twelve monthly maps. All four use a 2 km bandwidth and the same colour scale.

Each map is adjusted for the number of days in its quarter: 90, 91, 92 and 92. The colours show records per square kilometre per day, allowing for those small differences in length.


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](take-home-01/figures/quarters.png){fig-alt='Four quarterly accident density maps, adjusted for quarter length and shown on a common colour scale.' width=720}
:::
:::


Bangkok and Samut Sakhon show clear increases. Bangkok averaged 3.94 reports per day in the first quarter (January to March) and 6.17 in the last (October to December). Samut Sakhon rises from 0.39 to 1.67 per day. Pathum Thani changes much less, from 1.27 to 1.41. The maps show where these changes appear within each province. I would need more years to tell whether this happens regularly, and other data to explain the increase.

### 7.1 Did the rise in reports also mean more harm?

I separate reports into three groups: at least one death, injuries with no recorded death, and no recorded injury or death. Each report belongs to one group, even if several people were hurt.


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](take-home-01/figures/quarter-outcomes.png){fig-alt='Stacked bars show reports per day by outcome. All three categories rise from the first to the last quarter, with a smaller increase in fatal reports.' width=720}
:::
:::


From the first quarter to the last, reports involving injuries but no deaths rise from **2.99 to 4.63 per day**. Fatal reports rise more slowly, from 0.43 to 0.51 per day. The total rises from 8.14 to 12.32 per day. Emergency services would therefore need to consider the increase in injuries alongside the overall number of accidents.

The increase appears in all three agencies' records, with the Department of Highways accounting for 346 of the 400 additional reports. Reports marked rainy peak in July to September (160), then fall to 44 in October to December. Most reports in the last quarter are marked clear weather (1,079 of 1,133). Rain alone does not explain the rise in this file. I would need traffic counts and information on how much driving took place in each weather condition to investigate further.

### 7.2 Explore the months on the map

The red dots below pick out fatal reports. Use **Play** to step through the months, or select a province to see its counts. **Whole year** brings back the full pattern. The locations stay fixed; only the reports belonging to each month change.

```{=html}
<iframe id="th01-explorer" src="take-home-01/accident-explorer.html" title="Monthly accident map with playback and province comparisons" style="width:100%;height:1000px;border:0" loading="lazy"></iframe>
<script>
window.addEventListener('message', function(event) {
  const frame = document.getElementById('th01-explorer');
  if (event.source === frame.contentWindow && event.data?.type === 'th01-explorer-height') {
    const height = Number(event.data.height);
    if (Number.isFinite(height) && height > 0) frame.style.height = Math.ceil(height + 4) + 'px';
  }
});
</script>
```

[Open the map on its own](take-home-01/accident-explorer.html)

October has the most mapped reports (394), while **July has the most fatal reports (24)**. Use the province counts to compare places where overlapping dots are hard to read.

## 8. Do nearby accidents also happen close together in time?

A busy route may have accidents spread throughout the year. I wanted to check whether nearby accidents also tended to happen within a few days of each other. This is the second-order part of the analysis, which looks at pairs of events.

I use a Knox-style test to count pairs of accidents within 1 km and no more than 7 days apart. I chose these limits before seeing the results, as a way to check nearby accidents over one week. They are choices for this exercise, not official safety limits. Each pair counts once, although one accident can appear in several pairs. [Method: Knox test documentation](https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/surveillance/html/knox.html).

### 8.1 What am I comparing against?

I keep the locations in place and shuffle the accident times, then count the close pairs again. Times are only swapped among records from the same agency in the same calendar month. Repeating this 999 times gives me a range of counts to compare with the actual count.

This keeps each agency's road coverage and the monthly number of reports at each location. The dates and times available within each group also stay the same; only their assignment to locations changes. Busy dates and months therefore remain busy in the shuffled data.

The assumption is that swapping times within these groups gives a fair comparison when nearby accidents have no extra tendency to happen close together in time. Local traffic schedules, roadworks or reporting changes could make that assumption wrong.

I measure distance in a straight line and time from the recorded timestamps, so 7 days means 168 hours. I test for more close pairs, which makes this a one-sided test. The comparison uses only the observed locations and times within the six provinces in 2022. I do not estimate missing neighbours beyond those edges. The result applies to these records and still leaves out the 189 reports without coordinates. Finding no extra pairs would not establish that accidents are spatially random or that roads are safe.


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](take-home-01/figures/pair-test.png){fig-alt='Histogram of close-pair counts after shuffling times, with the actual observed count marked for comparison.' width=720}
:::
:::


The actual count is 2,204 pairs. The shuffled records average 2,091, so the actual count is 5.4% higher. The middle 95% of shuffled counts falls between 2,021 and 2,164. The actual count is above that range, with a one-sided p-value of 0.002. Nearby accidents happened within a week slightly more often than this comparison suggests. The test accounts for each agency's monthly pattern, but it cannot show that one accident caused another or that the result applies to every location.

The p-value describes how unusual the actual count is in this comparison. I count the shuffled patterns with at least as many close pairs, add the observed pattern, and divide by 1,000. The smallest possible p-value with 999 shuffles is 0.001.

### 8.2 Does the answer depend on choosing 1 km and 7 days?

I try 0.5, 1 and 2 km, each with time limits of 3, 7 and 14 days. That gives nine combinations, using the same shuffled records. This checks whether the result changes when I look a little closer, farther away, or over a different number of days.


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](take-home-exercise-01_files/figure-html/th01-scale-check-1.png){fig-alt='Nine combinations of distance and time thresholds, showing the percentage difference between observed close pairs and the shuffle average.' width=864}
:::
:::


The actual count is above the shuffled average in all nine comparisons. The difference is largest at 0.5 km and 3 days, at 17.1%, and smallest at 2 km and 14 days, at 2.7%. The shorter periods show larger percentage differences. After adjusting for the nine comparisons, eight have p-values below 0.05. The exception is 0.5 km and 7 days, at 0.055, so the evidence is weaker at that setting.

Trying more settings also gives more chances to find an unusual result. For an overall check, I measure each difference relative to how much the shuffled counts vary, then take the largest one. I do the same for every shuffle. This accounts for checking all nine settings and gives an overall p-value of 0.001.

### 8.3 Could repeated locations or reporting differences explain it?

I return to the 1 km / 7 day comparison and check three alternatives: remove one record from each possible duplicate pair; leave out pairs at exactly the same coordinates; and shuffle within month without separating agencies.


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}


|Check                                  | Observed pairs| Shuffle average| Difference (%)|p-value |
|:--------------------------------------|--------------:|---------------:|--------------:|:-------|
|Main: shuffle within agency and month  |          2,204|           2,091|            5.4|0.002   |
|Remove two possible duplicate reports  |          2,193|           2,082|            5.3|0.003   |
|Exclude pairs at identical coordinates |          2,145|           2,044|            4.9|0.003   |
|Shuffle within month only              |          2,204|           2,079|            6.0|0.001   |


:::
:::


The actual count stays about 5 to 6% above the shuffled average. Removing the possible duplicates leaves a difference of 5.3%; leaving out pairs at identical coordinates gives 4.9%. Those records do not explain the result on their own. Shuffling without separating agencies gives a slightly larger difference, so I keep agencies separate in the main test. Errors in coordinates or changes in local traffic and reporting during a month could still affect the result.

### 8.4 What changes when distance follows the roads?

For the same 426 matched reports in eastern Bangkok, I repeat the 1 km / 7 day comparison using distance along connected roads. The straight-line comparison below uses those same road matches. Road distances work in either direction on the mapped main roads and connectors; they do not represent driving time or include every local street.


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}


|Distance measured | Actual close pairs| Shuffle average|p-value |
|:-----------------|------------------:|---------------:|:-------|
|Straight line     |                563|             536|0.067   |
|Along roads       |                240|             246|0.676   |


:::
:::


Following the roads gives 240 close pairs, compared with about 246 after shuffling the times. Neither comparison gives clear evidence of extra clustering in time in this small area.

Routes 7 and 9 account for many reports here, but their timing looks much like the shuffled records. The earlier finding across all six provinces should not be assumed to apply to every concentration on the map.

## 9. What do these results say together?

Eastern Bangkok stands out on the density maps even when I change the amount of smoothing. The quarterly maps show that the later increase varies by province, with clear rises in Bangkok and Samut Sakhon. The pair test adds another finding: there are 5.4% more pairs within 1 km and 7 days than the shuffled comparison suggests. Removing possible duplicates and pairs at repeated locations gives similar results.

Routes 7 and 9 account for about 86% of the matched reports in the eastern Bangkok study area. The road-distance test gives no clear evidence of extra clustering in time there. The result across all six provinces therefore needs a closer check before it is used to guide action on these roads.

Pathum Thani and Samut Prakan account for just over half of fatal reports. Nonthaburi also deserves attention because many of its reports involve a death, despite its smaller total. Motorcycle reports and accidents overnight more often involve deaths too. The comparisons within agencies and vehicle groups give similar findings, though differences in traffic and reporting remain.

The three agencies cover selected roads, and the maps leave out the 189 Bangkok expressway reports without coordinates. Without traffic volumes or road lengths, I cannot compare the chance of an accident per journey. Shared or inaccurate coordinates may make accidents appear closer than they were, and straight-line distances ignore the road connections.

These results cover only 2022. More years would help show whether the late-year rise recurs. The weather labels do not support a simple rain explanation, but the file contains no measure of time spent driving in rain. Traffic changes, roadworks and reporting practices could still help explain the patterns. The casualty counts also depend on how each agency records and follows up an accident.

## 10. Recommendations for road safety

- Prioritise road safety inspections on Route 7 east of its junction with Route 9, and on nearby connecting ramps. Check signs, lane markings and visibility, then repair any defects found.

- Include locations of fatal accidents in Pathum Thani, Samut Prakan and Nonthaburi when choosing sites to inspect. Ranking places only by the number of reports would give Bangkok much more attention. Read the individual crash reports and inspect each site before deciding what to change.

- Check nighttime emergency coverage and motorcycle safety where fatal accidents occurred. Inspect lighting, visibility and road layout, and check dispatch records for delays. These are things to investigate; the accident records do not establish what caused the more severe outcomes.

- Review patrol and emergency-response coverage in Bangkok and Samut Sakhon, where reports rose late in 2022. Allow for the rise in injury reports as well as the total workload, and confirm the pattern in recent records before changing schedules.

- Have the reporting agencies review recent nearby accidents together each week. Flag repeated locations for site inspections, and test the 1 km / 7 day rule on later records before using it for automatic alerts.

- Require usable coordinates and a road-section reference in accident reports. Recover the locations of the 189 unmapped Bangkok expressway reports, and check new submissions for missing or implausible coordinates.

- Use the recorded injuries and deaths, along with traffic volumes, to decide which road improvements come first. Check conditions on site so each proposed change addresses a problem found on that road.

## 11. Sources and methods

- [Thailand Road Accident 2019–2022](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/thaweewatboy/thailand-road-accident-2019-2022), version 1; [Ministry of Transport source](https://datagov.mot.go.th/dataset/roadaccident). Only 2022 is analysed.
- [geoBoundaries country downloads](https://www.geoboundaries.org/countryDownloads.html), select Thailand and ADM1. The analysis uses the 2017 boundary representation, pinned to release commit 9469f09. Derived from OpenStreetMap/Wambacher; Open Database License 1.0.
- [National Statistical Office: Bangkok and Vicinities](https://www.nso.go.th/public/e-book/Statistical-Yearbook/SYB-2025/110/), for the six-province grouping.
- [spatstat: kernel-smoothed intensity](https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/spatstat.explore/html/density.ppp.html), for the density maps and edge correction.
- [Knox test for space-time interaction](https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/surveillance/html/knox.html), for the close-pair approach. Here I adapt the shuffling to preserve agency-month groups and compare several distance/time settings together.
- [OpenStreetMap: eastern Bangkok](https://www.openstreetmap.org/#map=12/13.7330/100.7140), with [contributor attribution and licence](https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright). The analysis uses roads as mapped on 1 January 2022. Open Database License 1.0.
